Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Emergency vs Reliability" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: Condition A emphasizes emergency protection and the safety signal (e.g., "Save lives at sea with a registered 406 MHz beacon that works when phone or radio fail."), Condition B emphasizes reliability and low cost (e.g., "Get a trusted, RTCM-certified beacon that delivers a distress signal when you need it most."). Both conditions include a price point and a "Buy" option. The test measures purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this beacon?") and stated reason for purchase.. Sample: 200 U.S. adults who own a boat or have been on a boat in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel. Randomly assigned 100 to Condition A and 100 to Condition B.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (binary) and stated reason for purchase (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will achieve a purchase intent rate of at least 5% and emergency protection will be the top stated reason.; T2: Condition B will achieve a purchase intent rate of at least 5% and reliability will be the top stated reason.. Decision rule: If Condition A achieves a purchase intent rate of at least 5% and emergency protection is the top stated reason, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual boat owners. If Condition B achieves a purchase intent rate of at least 5% and reliability is the top stated reason, pursue a reliability-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer sales.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or ACR’s ability to reach individual boat owners. Conduct the proposed Consumer Messaging Test to measure purchase intent and stated reasons before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources confirm the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or ACR’s ability to reach individual boat owners. Conduct the proposed Consumer Messaging Test to measure purchase intent and stated reasons before committing resources. Target customer: Individual boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts who need reliable emergency communication at sea.. Value proposition: A registered 406 MHz satellite distress beacon that provides a safety signal when phone or radio fail, meeting RTCM certification and NOAA requirements.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Messaging Test (Condition A vs Condition B) to determine whether emergency protection or reliability drives purchase intent.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers remain uncertain. Public sources do not show actual purchase behavior or demand.. Would change if: If the Consumer Messaging Test shows a purchase intent rate below 5% or reliability is the top stated reason, we would reconsider a consumer proposition or explore other alternatives.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand or ACR already reaches individual buyers, we would reassess the investment case.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Home-studio creators and individual producers who value professional-grade sound and want to be seen as serious artists.. Why behaviour changes: If creators perceive Neumann as the gold standard, they will choose it over cheaper alternatives, even if the price is higher, because they want to project credibility and quality in their work.. How value is captured: Neumann would capture value through premium pricing, limited-edition bundles, and brand extension that differentiates its professional line from mass-market competitors.. Assumptions: Home-studio creators have discretionary budget for studio equipment.; Brand reputation is a key purchase driver for this segment.; Professional quality is more important than price for this audience.. T2: Home-studio creators and individual buyers purchase Neumann products primarily for convenience and ease of use, not for professional quality. They seek equipment that integrates seamlessly with existing digital workflows and offers intuitive controls, so a differentiated proposition would increase adoption by reducing friction and time spent setting up. Who benefits: Home-studio creators and individual producers who want to record quickly and without technical hassle.. Why behaviour changes: If creators find Neumann products easy to set up and use, they will adopt them even if the price is higher, because they value time savings and workflow efficiency.. How value is captured: Neumann would capture value through bundled software, simplified setup guides, and marketing that emphasizes ease of use, potentially commanding higher margins than purely professional-grade products.. Assumptions: Creators prioritize workflow efficiency over raw sound quality.; Technical complexity deters purchase decisions.; Convenience is a primary purchase driver for this segment.. Predictions: Creators will show higher purchase intent for Neumann products that claim easy setup.; Willingness-to-pay will be higher for bundled or plug-and-play solutions than for standalone professional gear.; Surveys will show that convenience is a top factor in purchase decisions for this group..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Safety vs Lifestyle Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing EN 352 certification and safety compliance; Group B sees the same product described as a stylish, comfortable lifestyle accessory. Both groups see the same product image and price.. Sample: 300 adult consumers aged 18-45, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and stated primary reason for choosing the product (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and cite safety certification as the primary reason compared to Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and cite style and comfort as the primary reason compared to Group A.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two groups is at least 5 percentage points and the group with the higher intent also reports safety certification as the primary reason, we conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is at least 5 percentage points and the group with the higher intent also reports style and comfort, we conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the 5-point threshold, we conclude neither theory is supported and recommend further research.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes EN 352 certification and safety compliance, targeting both industrial and consumer markets. Use the proposed test to validate consumer willingness to pay for safety certification. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated result SYN-A concerns a wear test on appearance and does not address consumer motivations for purchasing hearing protection as a safety product. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safety product that meets regulatory standards (e.g., EN 352), because they trust certified safety labels and are willing to pay a premium for compliance.. Evidence: SYN-A.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes EN 352 certification and safety compliance, targeting both industrial and consumer markets. Use the proposed test to validate consumer willingness to pay for safety certification. Target customer: Consumers seeking safe, certified hearing protection for everyday use, including outdoor recreation, home improvement, and general daily activities.. Value proposition: A certified, safe product that meets regulatory standards, offering peace of mind and compliance, while leveraging Hellberg’s existing R&D and manufacturing capabilities to capture higher-margin consumer sales.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Proposition Test: Safety vs Lifestyle Messaging (300 participants, 4 weeks, €2,000) to measure purchase intent and primary purchase reason.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for hearing protection and the exact willingness to pay for certification are unknown. Competitor positioning and regulatory enforcement in consumer markets are also uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent between safety and lifestyle messaging, or if consumers cite style and comfort as the primary reason, we would reconsider the proposition and explore a lifestyle-focused segment. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Medical Necessity vs Fashion Home Protection" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are shown two versions of a product description for a Jotun multi‑surface kit (e.g., siding, deck, garden tools). Version A emphasizes marine and protective coatings as a medical necessity for home protection. Version B emphasizes marine and protective coatings as a fashion and functional home‑protection product. Both versions include a price of $150 and a willingness‑to‑pay question. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the kit.. Sample: 300 Norwegian homeowners and small business owners (150 per version) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region.. Measure: Purchase intent: binary (would purchase) and maximum price willing to pay. Secondary measure: stated reason for purchase (medical necessity vs fashion).. Predictions: T1: Version A will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness‑to‑pay than Version B, because the medical‑necessity framing resonates with homeowners seeking durable protection.; T2: Version B will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness‑to‑pay than Version A, because the fashion‑focused framing resonates with homeowners seeking multiple‑surface protection for different surfaces.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for Version A exceeds Version B by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 45% vs 35%), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing medical necessity. If purchase intent for Version B exceeds Version A by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with a fashion‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is below 10 percentage points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and continue focusing on existing B2B markets.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Jotun already serves both professional and DIY customers directly and through a network of Jotun Multicolor Centers, and there is no public evidence that consumers view marine coatings as a medical necessity for home protection. Instead, continue monitoring market trends and consider a phased approach, starting with a limited pilot to test Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Jotun already serves both professional and DIY customers directly and through a network of Jotun Multicolor Centers, and there is no public evidence that consumers view marine coatings as a medical necessity for home protection. Instead, continue monitoring market trends and consider a phased approach, starting with a limited pilot to test Target customer: Individual homeowners and small business owners seeking durable, long‑lasting protection for their homes.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition built on Jotun’s marine and protective coatings technology, positioned as a medical necessity for home protection, offering multiple‑surface kits and premium pricing.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Conduct a limited pilot test (e.g., a 6‑week online survey with randomized messaging) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a multi‑surface Jotun kit, and use the results to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer. Uncertainty: The evidence is limited to public sources and does not demonstrate consumer demand for marine coatings as a medical necessity or willingness to purchase multiple pairs for different surfaces.. Would change if: If a pilot test shows purchase intent for the medical‑necessity framing significantly exceeds the fashion‑focused framing (e.g., 45% vs 35%), we would proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for marine coatings as a medical necessity or willingness to pay a premium for multiple‑surface kits, we would reconsider investment.; If market conditions change significantly (e.g., a shift in consumer preferences or a new competitive threat), we would reassess the strategy.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Small-Scale Gardening vs Brand Reputation" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a differentiated small-scale garden tractor (e.g., Deere 110 model) priced at $200, emphasizing low-cost, reliable engineering. Group B sees the same tractor priced at $250, emphasizing brand reputation and reliability. Both groups are shown a neutral alternative at $150. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and reason for choice.. Sample: 200 homeowners aged 25–45, recruited via an online panel, balanced for geographic distribution.. Measure: Purchase intent score (Group A vs Group B) and reason for choice (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and cite low-cost, reliable equipment as the primary reason.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and cite brand reputation and reliability as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent exceeds Group B by at least 5 points (e.g., 7.5 vs 2.5) and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), proceed with a differentiated small‑scale proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points or not significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated small-scale gardening proposition targeting homeowners who need low-cost, reliable equipment. Use existing tractor engineering and dealer network to capture value. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Target customer: Homeowners aged 25–45 in the United States who currently lack affordable, efficient small‑scale gardening equipment.. Value proposition: A Deere‑branded, differentiated small‑scale garden tractor that leverages proven tractor engineering for durability and performance, sold through existing dealers at a premium price.. If Group A’s intent exceeds Group B by at least 5 points and is statistically significant, proceed with product development.. Uncertainty: The size of the homeowner market in 1962 and whether they are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition are uncertain. Also uncertain is the competitive landscape and whether Deere’s brand reputation is strong enough to be a. Would change if: If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the two groups or if the difference is less than 5 points, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of no expansion or a different customer segment.; If new evidence shows that homeowners in 1962 primarily prefer cheaper alternatives or that Deere’s brand reputation is weak, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of a different strategy.. Just 7% of Gen Z adults say they have always used earplugs at loud music events in the last 12 months, while only one in five said they often wear them. Test "Premium vs. Non-Premium Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from individual buyers who have purchased Neumann products in the past. They are shown two identical product pages for a new Neumann microphone, one with premium messaging emphasizing brand prestige and compatibility with existing professional equipment, and one with non-premium messaging emphasizing quality and performance. Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay and whether they would purchase.. Sample: 300 individual buyers who have purchased Neumann products in the past, randomly assigned to two groups of 150 each.. Measure: Maximum price willingness-to-pay (WTP) and purchase intent (binary: would buy).. Predictions: T1: Group with premium messaging will show higher WTP and higher purchase intent than group with non-premium messaging.; T2: Group with non-premium messaging will show higher WTP and higher purchase intent than group with premium messaging.. Decision rule: If premium messaging group WTP is at least 20% higher than non-premium messaging group WTP, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T1 is supported and a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators is recommended. If non-premium messaging group WTP is at least 20% higher, then T2 is supported and a differentiated proposition for individual buyers is recommended. If neither difference is statistically significant, the status quo of a single professional range for all customers remains appropriate.. Cost: 5000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers, emphasizing brand prestige and compatibility with existing professional equipment. T1: Individual boat owners purchase personal distress beacons primarily for legal compliance and insurance requirements, so a consumer proposition will succeed if it is marketed as a required item for boat registration, not as a fashion item. Who benefits: ACR Electronics and its B2B customers gain higher volume sales and can charge a premium for compliance-focused features.. Why behaviour changes: Compliance and insurance requirements make the beacon a necessary purchase for boat owners, shifting purchase from discretionary to mandatory.. How value is captured: ACR captures value through higher unit volume and premium pricing for compliance features, while insurance companies may subsidize or require the device.. Assumptions: Boat registration and insurance requirements exist and are enforced in late 2002 marine markets.; Compliance is the primary driver of purchase, not lifestyle or fashion.; ACR can adapt existing beacon technology to meet compliance standards without major redesign.. Predictions: In markets with strict boat registration and insurance requirements, purchase intent for a consumer beacon will be higher than in markets without such requirements.; Surveyed boat owners will cite compliance as the main reason for buying a beacon.; ACR's sales will be concentrated in regions with strong marine compliance regulations..

T2: Individual boat owners purchase personal distress beacons primarily for lifestyle and safety awareness, viewing them as a status symbol and a way to ensure personal safety, so a consumer proposition will succeed if it is marketed as a premium, design‑focused product. Who benefits: ACR Electronics gains higher margin sales and brand extension, while consumers gain a product they perceive as desirable and protective.. Why behaviour changes: Growing consumer awareness of marine safety and desire for premium, stylish gear shifts purchase from utilitarian to lifestyle, making price and design important.. How value is captured: ACR captures value through premium pricing, brand extension, and potential licensing of design elements to other consumer products.. Assumptions: Lifestyle and safety awareness are significant drivers of consumer purchase in marine markets.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for design and brand associated with safety.; ACR can adapt its technology to meet consumer design expectations without compromising performance.. Predictions: In markets where lifestyle and safety awareness are high, purchase intent for a consumer beacon will be higher than in markets where compliance is the primary driver.; Surveyed boat owners will cite lifestyle and safety as the main reasons for buying a beacon.; ACR's sales will be concentrated in regions with strong lifestyle and safety‑focused marine markets..
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

Why behaviour changes: They would switch from manual weighing to a device that provides a numeric body-fat measurement, reducing guesswork and enabling data-driven choices.. How value is captured: Tanita would sell the device at a premium price through retail or online channels, capturing margin on the analyser and potentially additional services like data tracking or coaching.. T2: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a medical device for specific health conditions (e.g., heart disease, diabetes) because they already use bathroom scales and trust medical evidence. Test "Home Body-Fat Analyser Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and purchase intent measurement.. Sample: 500 adults (18-65) recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender to reflect the target market.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and stated reason for purchase (health monitoring vs. medical/health risk).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and stated health monitoring as primary reason among participants exposed to health messaging.; T2: Higher purchase intent and stated medical/health risk as primary reason among participants exposed to medical messaging.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for health monitoring exceeds medical/health risk by at least 10 percentage points among the health messaging group, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting fitness enthusiasts. If the difference is less than 10 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and focus on B2B expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Evidence shows consumers already use bathroom scales and keep track of body composition, but it does not show they would purchase a home body-fat analyser specifically for health monitoring or pay a premium price. Conduct the proposed purchase intent test to validate demand before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Evidence shows consumers already use bathroom scales and keep track of body composition, but it does not show they would purchase a home body-fat analyser specifically for health monitoring or pay a premium price. Conduct the proposed purchase intent test to validate demand before committing resources. Target customer: Fitness enthusiasts and health-conscious individuals who already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health insights.. Value proposition: A home body-fat analyser marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management, leveraging Tanita’s medical credibility and existing consumer scale distribution.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 6‑week online purchase intent test with 500 adults, comparing health‑monitoring messaging against medical‑health‑risk messaging.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for health‑focused body‑fat measurement and whether consumers would pay a premium price for a home device.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for health monitoring significantly exceeds medical‑health‑risk messaging by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or low intent, reconsider expansion or partner with retailers instead of developing a consumer product.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Households will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they view lawn tractors as a convenient, low‑cost way to manage small gardens, and they trust the brand for durability and reliability. Who benefits: Homeowners with small gardens who need easy, affordable gardening solutions.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from manual or manual‑assisted tasks to a machine that can be operated by one person, reducing effort and time.. How value is captured: Deere captures value through premium pricing for a differentiated model, higher margins from sales, and potential attachment sales of accessories.. Assumptions: Households in 1962 have limited budget for gardening equipment.; They are willing to pay a premium for a brand they perceive as reliable.; The market size for small‑scale gardening is large enough to justify production.. Predictions: If offered a differentiated lawn tractor, a measured percentage of households will express intent to purchase within a specified timeframe.; Sales of the differentiated model will exceed sales of a standard model in the same period.; Customer surveys will show higher satisfaction with ease of use and reliability compared to competitors..

T2: Households will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they view lawn tractors as a status symbol and a way to signal modernity and ownership, leading them to purchase multiple units for different tasks. Who benefits: Affluent homeowners and small‑farm owners who use tractors for multiple purposes and seek to display ownership.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from a single, basic task to a versatile machine that can be used for gardening, mowing, and other outdoor work, increasing frequency of use.. How value is captured: Deere captures value through premium pricing for a differentiated model, higher volume sales from multiple attachments, and potential licensing of the brand for consumer products.. Assumptions: Affluent households in 1962 are willing to invest in multiple gardening tools.; The brand is associated with prestige and modernity.; There is a large enough market for multiple‑unit purchases.. Predictions: If offered a differentiated proposition, a measured percentage of households will purchase multiple units within a specified timeframe.; Sales of the differentiated model will be driven by attachment sales rather than a single unit.; Surveys will show higher willingness to pay for a brand perceived as prestigious..

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offering and choice-based conjoint analysis.. Sample: 500 households in the United States who have a small garden or garden space, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: 1) Intent to purchase a differentiated lawn tractor (binary: would buy). 2) Willingness to pay a premium (percentage willing to pay at $1,200 vs $800). 3) Number of units intended to purchase (binary: would buy one, two, or three).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% will express intent to purchase a differentiated model, and willingness to pay premium will be at least 10% higher than for a standard model.; T2: At least 30% will express intent to purchase multiple units (two or three), and willingness to pay premium will be at least 10% higher than for a standard model.. Decision rule: If intent to purchase a differentiated model exceeds 30% and willingness to pay premium is at least 10% higher than for a standard model, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition. If intent is below 20% or premium willingness to pay is not significantly higher, do not invest.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows a growing market for lawn and garden equipment (76% sales rise, 1960‑99), and the 4010 model was the most popular, indicating demand. However, no source shows households are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated brand or that they view tractors as a status symbol. A low‑cost test is needed to measure intent and willingness Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows a growing market for lawn and garden equipment (76% sales rise, 1960‑99) and the 4010 model was the most popular, indicating demand. However, no source shows households are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated brand or that they view tractors as a status symbol. A low‑cost test is needed to measure intent and willingness. Target customer: Households with small gardens who need easy, affordable gardening solutions.. Value proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor offering convenience, reliability, and brand trust, positioned as a practical solution for small‑scale gardening tasks.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (500 households, $18,000, 10 weeks) to validate intent to purchase and willingness to pay premium.. Uncertainty: The willingness of households to pay a premium for a differentiated brand and their motivation to purchase as a status symbol are unknown. The test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the test shows intent to purchase below 20% or willingness to pay premium is not significantly higher than for a standard model, the investment would be reconsidered.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for multiple‑unit purchases or premium pricing, the strategy would shift toward a differentiated proposition targeting multiple uses.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Sample: 500 adults aged 18-45, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to ensure representativeness.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP in the Health Messaging condition compared to the Style Messaging condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP in the Style Messaging condition compared to the Health Messaging condition.. Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Status vs. Practicality" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel offers to individual consumers in a small town. Each participant sees one offer describing a Deere lawn tractor positioned differently: (A) as a practical, low-cost gardening tool for small gardens; (B) as a status symbol for modern home ownership. Both offers include the same price point. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the offer and. Sample: 50 participants, recruited from a local community, balanced for age and gender. Each participant views one offer and provides a binary purchase decision.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and stated willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars for the differentiated feature. Secondary measure: self-reported reason for purchase (status vs. practicality).. Predictions: T1: Participants viewing the practical offer will have higher purchase intent and WTP than those viewing the status offer, indicating demand driven by cost and practicality.; T2: Participants viewing the status offer will have higher purchase intent and WTP than those viewing the practical offer, indicating demand driven by status and lifestyle.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two offers is statistically significant (p < 0.05) and the status offer achieves at least 15% higher intent than the practical offer, proceed with a differentiated status proposition. If the difference is not significant, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows a 76% rise in lawn and garden equipment sales in 1962, indicating overall consumer interest, but it does not demonstrate that consumers choose Deere over competitors or that a differentiated proposition would increase purchases. A limited test is needed to confirm demand. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows a 76% rise in lawn and garden equipment sales in 1962, indicating overall consumer interest, but it does not demonstrate that consumers choose Deere over competitors or that a differentiated proposition would increase purchases. A limited test is needed to confirm demand. Target customer: Small‑homeowners and suburban gardeners who purchase small‑scale gardening equipment for practical, low‑cost tasks.. Value proposition: A differentiated Deere lawn tractor positioned as a reliable, cost‑effective solution for small gardens, leveraging the company’s brand reputation for durability.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test: Status vs. Practicality to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated offer.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and whether Deere can capture higher margins without cannibalizing B2B sales remain uncertain. Evidence of consumer preference for Deere over competitors is also lacking.. Would change if: If the test shows a statistically significant difference in purchase intent between the practical and status offers, and the status offer achieves at least 15% higher intent, we would reconsider investing in a differentiated proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for Deere’s brand or a clear willingness to pay premium prices, we would strengthen the case for a differentiated proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Homeowners will adopt Jotun's marine and protective coatings for non‑marine use cases because they perceive the technology as high‑performance and safety‑critical, leading them to purchase directly online and pay a premium for durability. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and small‑business owners seeking reliable protection for exterior surfaces.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from generic paints to a trusted marine brand when they view the product as a medical‑grade, long‑lasting solution for weather and fouling resistance.. How value is captured: Jotun captures value through direct‑to‑consumer sales, premium pricing justified by performance claims, and potential co‑branding royalties.. Assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for marine‑grade protection.; Online purchase channels can reach and convert this segment effectively.; Jotun's brand reputation in marine markets transfers to consumer perception.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from multiple brands to a single provider when they perceive consistency and brand reliability, reducing decision‑fatigue and increasing purchase intent.. How value is captured: Jotun captures value through increased volume sales via existing retail channels, reduced marketing spend, and potential co‑branding royalties from consumer products.. Assumptions: Homeowners value brand consistency across products.; Jotun's existing retail presence (Jotun Multicolor Centers) can be leveraged for consumer sales.; Brand loyalty to one provider outweighs price sensitivity for exterior protection.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners will show at least 60% prefer purchasing from one brand for all exterior needs.; Sales growth in Jotun's decorative segment will be driven by repeat purchases rather than new customers.; Jotun's retail channels will show higher average order value than direct‑to‑consumer sales..

Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.; Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safety product that meets regulatory standards, because they already use hearing protection in work and industrial settings and trust certified standards. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand reputation tied to EN 352 certification.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently use generic earplugs without certification; a differentiated proposition that clearly states EN 352 compliance would shift their purchase from generic to certified products.. How value is captured: Value is captured through higher margins on certified products sold directly to consumers or through partnerships that leverage the certification.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of EN 352 certification and its relevance to hearing protection.; Regulatory compliance is a primary purchase driver for hearing protection.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for certified products.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated product with EN 352 certification, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15% higher than for an unbranded generic earplug.; Surveyed consumers will cite certification as the primary reason for choosing the product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a lifestyle or fashion accessory, because they already wear headbands and earplugs for recreational and leisure activities, and are willing to pay for stylish, comfortable designs. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety benefits by reaching a new consumer segment with higher average transaction value and brand association beyond industrial safety.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently view hearing protection as functional gear; a proposition that frames it as a fashion item or lifestyle accessory would shift their purchase from utilitarian to aspirational.. How value is captured: Value is captured through premium pricing, direct-to-consumer sales, and brand extension that differentiates from industrial safety brands.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with recreational activities and are open to styling.; Fashion and lifestyle are primary purchase drivers for earplugs among younger consumers.; Hellberg can design and market a product that appeals to fashion-conscious buyers without compromising safety performance.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated product positioned as a fashion accessory, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 20% higher than for an unbranded generic earplug.; Surveyed consumers will cite style and comfort as the primary reason for choosing the product..

Test "Choice Experiment for Home Protection Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with two product variants and a brand attribute condition.. Sample: 200 Norwegian homeowners (recruited via panel) who have completed a home improvement survey in the past 12 months.. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) for each product variant (€). 2) Self‑reported importance of Norwegian heritage (1‑10 scale). 3) Intent to purchase (binary: would buy).. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP for the Norwegian‑heritage variant and higher purchase intent than for the generic marine variant.; T2: Higher WTP for the generic marine variant and higher purchase intent than for the Norwegian‑heritage variant.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the Norwegian‑heritage variant exceeds the WTP for the generic marine variant by at least €15 and the purchase intent difference is ≥ 5 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated Norwegian‑heritage consumer proposition. If the generic variant’. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Jotun already offers direct‑to‑consumer sales and is available on its website, but it does not demonstrate that homeowners choose Jotun for home protection. A choice experiment is needed to test willingness to pay for Norwegian heritage versus generic marine variants. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show Jotun already offers direct‑to‑consumer sales and is available on its website, but they do not demonstrate that homeowners choose Jotun for home protection. A choice experiment is needed to test willingness to pay for Norwegian heritage versus generic marine variants. Target customer: Individual homeowners and small business owners in Scandinavia who need home protection for buildings.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition built on Jotun’s marine and protective coatings technology, positioned as a reliable, durable solution for home protection, leveraging the brand’s existing B2B reputation and direct‑to‑consumer sales.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed choice experiment (200 homeowners, two product variants, €18,000 budget, 6 weeks) to measure willingness to pay for Norwegian heritage versus generic marine variants.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for home protection in Scandinavia and whether homeowners are willing to pay a premium for a Norwegian‑heritage brand are unknown. The soft consumer market in Scandinavia also adds uncertainty.. Would change if: If the choice experiment shows the Norwegian‑heritage variant has significantly higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than the generic marine variant, proceed with a differentiated Norwegian‑heritage consumer proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for home protection or a large, untapped market, reconsider the investment.; If the existing B2B segment remains the primary revenue driver, the case for a consumer proposition weakens.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Jotun Home Protection Consumer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a simulated purchase decision.. Sample: 300 Norwegian homeowners (18-65) who have completed a home improvement project in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) for a differentiated Jotun home protection product at three price points (€30, €50, €80). 2) Choice frequency: which product they would select for a home protection project.. Test "Segmented Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product concepts: (A) a lifestyle-style hearing protection line (e.g., fashion-forward earplugs with multiple colors and designs) and (B) a specialized hearing protection line for specific high-frequency activities (e.g., construction, outdoor recreation). Participants are randomly assigned to view either concept first or both concepts.. Sample: 500 adults in Sweden and Germany, recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender to reflect target consumer segments.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Viewing the lifestyle concept first will increase purchase intent by at least 15% compared to viewing the specialized concept first, and WTP for the lifestyle concept will be at least 20% higher than for the specialized concept.; T2: Viewing the specialized concept first will increase purchase intent by at least 20% compared to viewing the lifestyle concept first, and WTP for the specialized concept will be at least 30% higher than for the lifestyle concept.. Decision rule: If the lifestyle concept's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than the specialized concept's purchase intent, proceed with a differentiated lifestyle proposition. If the specialized concept's purchase intent is at least 20 percentage points higher, proceed with a differentiated specialized proposition. If neither difference meets the thresholds, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and continue focusing on the current hearing and face protection portfolio.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence does not demonstrate that consumers view hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory or that they are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition. The market is small and unproven, and Hellberg's existing hearing and face protection portfolio serves a clear B2B/industrial need. Continue focusing on the current portfolio Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated wear test (SYN-B) shows that a softer, better-fitting protector did not increase wear frequency compared to a standard one. This does not address whether consumers view hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory or whether they are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-B.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence does not demonstrate that consumers view hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory or that they are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition. The market is small and unproven, and Hellberg's existing hearing and face protection portfolio serves a clear B2B/industrial need. Target customer: Consumers who currently purchase hearing protection for industrial, job, or hobby use cases (e.g., construction workers, outdoor enthusiasts, hobbyists).. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory or specialized solution for specific high-frequency activities, leveraging Hellberg's design expertise and brand reputation.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Conduct a limited, low-cost test (e.g., a 10-week online survey with randomized exposure to lifestyle vs. specialized concepts) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing to a full product launch.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for hearing protection in Europe is unknown, and there is no public evidence of consumer willingness to pay a premium for differentiated products. The simulated wear test (SYN-B) does not address consumerPer. Would change if: If a test shows a lifestyle concept achieving at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent than a specialized concept, or if willingness to pay for the lifestyle concept is at least 20% above the baseline, the recommendation would; If a test shows a specialized concept achieving at least 20 percentage points higher purchase intent than a lifestyle concept, or if willingness to pay for the specialized concept is at least 30% above the baseline, the recommendation would; If new public evidence shows a significant decline in the hearing protection market in Europe in 2023, the recommendation would be to maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they view hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory that signals health awareness and safety commitment, leading them to purchase multiple pairs for different activities. Who benefits: Consumers seeking personal safety and style; Hellberg Safety benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty.. Why behaviour changes: Shifting perception from a medical necessity to a fashion and lifestyle item reduces price sensitivity and increases willingness to own multiple units.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium for design and brand differentiation, sell through retail or direct-to-consumer channels, and build a recurring revenue model with accessories.. Assumptions: Consumers currently perceive hearing protection as purely functional.; A lifestyle positioning can be effectively communicated to target demographics.; Retail or online channels can reach the intended consumer base.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate higher purchase intent for a lifestyle-branded hearing protection product compared to a purely functional product.; Willingness to pay will be higher for a differentiated proposition than for a standard industrial product.; Purchase intent will correlate with self-reported health-consciousness levels..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they need hearing protection for specific, high-frequency activities (e.g., construction, outdoor recreation) where standard earplugs are insufficient, creating a clear functional need that a differentiated product can address. Who benefits: Consumers with specific safety needs; Hellberg Safety benefits by offering a specialized product that meets those needs and can command higher margins.. Why behaviour changes: When a product directly solves a specific, high-frequency safety concern, consumers are more likely to purchase it than a generic hearing-protection item.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price the differentiated product at a premium, sell through specialized channels (e.g., construction suppliers, outdoor retailers), and offer accessories or upgrades for specific use cases.. Assumptions: There is a measurable segment of consumers who currently lack adequate protection for specific activities.; These consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that directly addresses their safety need.; Hellberg can differentiate its product with features tailored to those activities.. Predictions: Consumers will show higher purchase intent for a differentiated product marketed for specific activities compared to a generic product.; Willingness to pay will be higher for a product positioned as a solution to a specific safety concern.; Sales conversion will be higher in channels that target specific industries or activities..

case.question: It is mid-1962. Should Deere & Company develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its tractor engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
In 1869, Charles began to introduce marketing centers and independent retail dealers to advance the company's sales nationwide.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, market demand, competitive landscape, and technical feasibility.; Evidence must address whether a differentiated proposition would create measurable demand or value capture.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, homeowner gardening).; 2) Expand existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B/agricultural markets.; 4) Partner with or license Deere technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling directly.; 5) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners) with a differentiated proposition..

T1: Homeowners will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they see the tractor as a specialized tool for a specific use case (e.g., small-scale landscaping, gardening), and they value the engineering reputation and reliability associated with John Deere. Who benefits: Homeowners who need a reliable, specialized lawn and garden tractor; Deere benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty.. Why behaviour changes: If homeowners perceive the tractor as a purpose-built solution rather than a generic farm machine, they will be willing to pay more for features and performance tailored to their needs.. How value is captured: Deere can sell through independent dealers with a differentiated product line, commanding higher price points than standard agricultural equipment.. Assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 have the disposable income to purchase a dedicated lawn and garden tractor.; Deere's engineering reputation is sufficient to differentiate the product from competitors.; Independent dealers can effectively promote and service a differentiated consumer proposition.. Predictions: In a test market, homeowners will express willingness to pay a premium price for a John Deere lawn and garden tractor compared to an equivalent competitor.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed as a specialized tool rather than a general farm tractor.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with higher homeowner density and interest in outdoor recreation..

T2: Homeowners will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they view the tractor as a status symbol and a status signal, indicating modernity and ownership of a premium outdoor space, leading them to seek a brand that reflects their lifestyle. Who benefits: Affluent homeowners who use outdoor spaces as a status display; Deere benefits by selling a premium, brand‑rich product that commands higher margins.. Why behaviour changes: If homeowners perceive the tractor as a status item, they will choose a brand that signals modernity and ownership of a well‑kept outdoor area, even if the functional need is limited.. How value is captured: Deere can price the product at a premium, sell through high‑margin independent dealers, and build brand loyalty that justifies higher prices.. Assumptions: Affluent homeowners in 1962 have discretionary income to purchase a status‑oriented lawn and garden tractor.; Brand perception of modernity and ownership is a significant purchase driver for this segment.; Independent dealers can effectively promote a brand‑rich consumer proposition.. Predictions: In a test market, homeowners will show higher purchase intent for a brand positioned as a status item compared to a functional, utilitarian proposition.; Willingness to pay will be higher for a product marketed as a lifestyle accessory rather than a tool.; Sales will be concentrated in affluent suburban and urban markets where status signaling is more prominent..

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 200 U.S. homeowners (ages 30-65) recruited via an online panel, stratified by region (suburban, urban) and household income.. Measure: 1) WTP to purchase a John Deere lawn and garden tractor priced at $1,200 (functional proposition). 2) WTP to purchase the same tractor priced at $1,500 (status proposition). 3) Intent to recommend the product to a friend.. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP for the $1,200 functional proposition than for the $1,500 status proposition, and higher purchase intent than for a competitor's product.; T2: Higher WTP for the $1,500 status proposition than for the $1,200 functional proposition, and higher purchase intent than for a competitor's product.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the functional proposition exceeds the WTP for the status proposition by at least $200 (e.g., $1,200 vs $1,500), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale landscaping. If the status proposition's WTP exceeds the functional proposition's by at least $200, pursue a status‑oriented proposition. If both propositions are equally willing to pay, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale landscaping and homeowner gardening, leveraging Deere's engineering reputation and existing dealer network. Begin with a limited pilot to test willingness to pay and demand before full-scale rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale landscaping and homeowner gardening, leveraging Deere's engineering reputation and existing dealer network. Begin with a limited pilot to test willingness to pay and demand before full-scale rollout. Target customer: Homeowners (ages 30-65) in suburban and urban areas with small gardens who value reliability and are willing to pay a premium for a specialized tool.. Value proposition: A purpose-built John Deere lawn and garden tractor that combines Deere's engineering expertise with features tailored to small-scale landscaping, marketed through independent dealers to capture higher margins.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Proposition Preference Test (200 homeowners, $18,000, 10 weeks) to compare willingness to pay for functional vs. status propositions.. Uncertainty: Demand for a differentiated consumer proposition is uncertain; evidence shows Deere already produced 1,000 units in 1963, but no source confirms homeowner purchase intent or willingness to pay.. Would change if: If the test shows the status proposition's willingness to pay exceeds the functional proposition by at least $200, we would shift focus to a status‑oriented proposition.; If no test is conducted, we would maintain the status quo of no expansion and continue focusing on B2B/agricultural markets.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Why behaviour changes: They currently rely on manual methods or generic scales; a device that gives precise body-fat data will motivate them to measure more frequently and follow progress.. Test "Home Body-Fat Analyser Purchase Intent Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and purchase intent questions.. Sample: 200 respondents: 100 fitness enthusiasts (recruited via fitness forums) and 100 pregnant women (recruited via maternal health groups). Randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions.. Measure: Purchase intent: binary (would buy) and willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Fitness enthusiasts exposed to progress-tracking messaging will have a purchase intent rate of at least 30% and a WTP at least 20% higher than pregnant women.; T2: Pregnant women exposed to pregnancy/postpartum messaging will have a purchase intent rate of at least 25% and a WTP at least 20% higher than fitness enthusiasts.. Decision rule: If either condition meets its threshold (e.g., fitness enthusiasts: purchase intent ≥30% and WTP ≥20% higher; pregnant women: purchase intent ≥25% and WTP ≥20% higher), proceed with a limited consumer launch. If neither meets its threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Evidence shows Tanita already has a stand-on body-fat analyser for clinics and health clubs, and there is no public source from 1993 showing that fitness enthusiasts would purchase a home body-fat analyser. A limited pilot test (e.g., purchase intent survey) is needed before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public sources from 1993 show Tanita already has a stand-on body-fat analyser for clinics and health clubs, and there is no evidence that fitness enthusiasts or pregnant women would purchase a home body-fat analyser. A limited pilot test (e.g., purchase intent survey) is needed before committing resources. case.question: It is mid-1962. Should Deere & Company develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its tractor engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
Of the "10" series John Deere tractors introduced in 1960, the 4010 was by far the most popular, with more than 58,000 units sold from 1960 to 1963.
In 1869, Charles began to introduce marketing centers and independent retail dealers to advance the company's sales nationwide.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, market demand, competitive landscape, and technical feasibility.; Evidence must address whether a differentiated proposition would create measurable demand or value capture.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, homeowner gardening).; 2) Expand existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B/agricultural markets.; 4) Partner with or license Deere technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling directly.; 5) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners) with a differentiated proposition..

Who benefits: Households with small gardens that need to clear grass, mow, or move debris.. Why behaviour changes: They change behaviour from manual or hired labor to self‑service equipment because the tractor is inexpensive, easy to operate, and can be used for multiple tasks.. How value is captured: Deere captures value by selling a differentiated consumer line at a premium price through independent dealers, leveraging its tractor engineering to offer durability and performance.. Assumptions: Households in 1962 have small gardens and need gardening equipment.; The cost of a garden tractor is low enough to be affordable for most households.; Independent dealers can effectively distribute and service consumer tractors.. Predictions: In 1962, households with small gardens will purchase garden tractors at a higher rate than households without small gardens.; Sales of a differentiated Deere consumer line will be higher in regions with higher garden ownership rates.; Customers will be willing to pay a premium for features that improve usability and durability..

T2: Households will adopt garden tractors if they perceive them as a status symbol or a status signal, because they want to demonstrate financial stability or modernity in their home. Who benefits: Affluent households that view gardening equipment as a reflection of taste and economic success.. Why behaviour changes: They change behaviour from manual labor to self-service equipment because owning a garden tractor signals modernity and ability to manage a home, leading to higher purchase frequency.. How value is captured: Deere captures value by positioning a differentiated consumer line as a premium, status‑oriented product, selling through specialty retailers that emphasize design and brand prestige.. Assumptions: Affluent households in 1962 are willing to pay a premium for garden tractors.; Garden tractors are perceived as a status symbol rather than a utilitarian tool.; Specialty retailers can effectively market and sell a differentiated consumer line.. Predictions: Affluent households will purchase garden tractors at a higher rate than average households.; Sales of a differentiated Deere line will be concentrated in regions with higher income levels.; Customers will be willing to pay a premium for features that enhance aesthetic appeal and brand prestige..

case.question: Should Neumann develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and other individual buyers, beyond its existing professional studio offering, or keep one professional range for everyone? What evidence would justify either choice?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: The Neumann Home Studio Academy offers high-quality tutorial videos on various aspects of recording via a dedicated website and an associated YouTube channel
The videos, which have met with an extremely positive response in recent years, are often described by viewers as being the best in this field.
The home studio segment is now responsible for more than half of total studio vertical revenue and the numbers are climbing.

As restrictions subsided and individuals returned to their normal lives, the pro audio equipment market for home studio content creation has been forced to re-stabilise from unsustainable pandemic levels. events.text: Objective: Determine whether Neumann should create a differentiated product or service proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers, beyond its existing professional studio range, or keep a single professional range for all customers.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Search budget of 8 keyword searches.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of current individual buyer reach and demand.; Alternatives must include no expansion, product redesign, different route to buyers, and different customer group.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers (e.g., specialized microphones, monitors, or bundled solutions).; 2) Keep a single professional range for all customers (no differentiation).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional studio products.; 4) Change route to buyers: introduce a direct-to-consumer online channel without product differentiation.; 5) Target a different customer group: shift focus to music producers, podcasters, or other non‑professional users..

T1: Home-studio creators and individual buyers value professional-grade audio quality and brand reputation, so they will purchase Neumann products even if the price is higher than consumer alternatives, because they view studio equipment as a necessary investment in their craft. Who benefits: Home-studio creators and individual creators who produce music, podcasts, or content.. Why behaviour changes: These creators perceive high-quality audio as essential for professional results, and they trust Neumann's reputation for audio excellence, leading them to choose Neumann over lower-priced competitors.. How value is captured: Neumann captures value through premium pricing, brand loyalty, and potential cross-selling of accessories or services.. Assumptions: Creators are willing to pay a premium for professional-grade audio.; Neumann's brand reputation is strong enough to justify higher prices.; The market size for home-studio creators is large enough to support a differentiated proposition.. Predictions: Creators will show higher purchase intent when presented with a differentiated Neumann product.; Willingness to pay for a differentiated product will be above the average price of consumer alternatives.; Brand perception will correlate with purchase decisions..

T2: Home-studio creators and individual buyers prioritize convenience and ease of use, so they will adopt Neumann products if they offer integrated solutions or plug-and-play features that reduce setup time and technical barriers. Who benefits: Home-studio creators and individual creators who lack technical expertise or time for complex setup.. Why behaviour changes: These creators value products that can be quickly set up and used without requiring advanced knowledge, making Neumann's integrated solutions more attractive than standalone equipment.. How value is captured: Neumann captures value through higher unit volume, reduced customer support costs, and potential cross-selling of accessories or services that complement the integrated setup.. Assumptions: Creators are willing to pay for convenience and ease of use.; Integrated solutions reduce the learning curve for new equipment.; The market size for creators who value convenience is large enough to support a differentiated proposition.. Predictions: Creators will show higher purchase intent when presented with integrated Neumann products.; Willingness to pay for convenience features will be above the price of standalone equipment.; Adoption rates for integrated products will be higher than for standalone products..

T1 supports, from neumann-academy (company_assertion): "The Neumann Home Studio Academy offers high-quality tutorial videos on various aspects of recording via a dedicated website and an associated YouTube channel". Does not show: It does not provide evidence of purchase intent, willingness to pay, or brand reputation impact on buying decisions..

T2 supports, from neumann-futuresource-2018 (market_fact): "The home studio segment is now responsible for more than half of total studio vertical revenue and the numbers are climbing.". Does not show: It does not provide evidence that creators specifically value convenience or that Neumann's integrated solutions are preferred over standalone equipment..

Test "Home-Studio Creator Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized product exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 200 home-studio creators (music producers, podcasters, content creators) recruited via social media and industry forums.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) and WTP (maximum price). 2) Preference for integrated vs standalone features (yes/no).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for a differentiated Neumann product (e.g., bundled microphone + monitor).; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for an integrated Neumann product (e.g., plug-and-play bundle).. Decision rule: If the integrated product (T2) achieves a purchase intent rate of at least 30% and a WTP above €500, proceed to develop an integrated proposition. If the differentiated product (T1) meets the same thresholds, develop a differentiated proposition. If neither meets thresholds, keep the single professional range.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers, focusing on premium audio quality and brand reputation. Use the existing Home Studio Academy platform to promote the proposition and gather purchase intent data. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers, emphasizing premium audio quality and brand reputation. Use the existing Home Studio Academy platform to promote the proposition and gather purchase intent data. Target customer: Home-studio creators and individual creators who produce music, podcasts, or content.. Value proposition: A premium, integrated or bundled Neumann product that delivers professional-grade audio quality and leverages Neumann's brand reputation, offering creators a trusted solution for their recording needs.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Home-Studio Creator Preference Test to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated Neumann product.. Uncertainty: The size of the home-studio creator market and their willingness to pay a premium for Neumann's brand reputation are uncertain. Additionally, the impact of convenience features on purchase decisions is not yet established.. Would change if: If the test shows that creators prioritize convenience and are willing to pay significantly above the price of standalone equipment, we would shift focus to an integrated or plug-and-play proposition.; If new evidence shows that home-studio creators are highly price-sensitive and prefer lower-priced alternatives, we would reconsider the premium positioning.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Fashion vs. Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel representing both work/industrial hearing protection users (n=300) and leisure/active consumers (n=300). Each participant sees one of two product descriptions: (A) EN 352-certified headband marketed for outdoor recreation, emphasizing safety and regulatory compliance; (B) same headband marketed as a fashion, comfortable accessory for outdoor recreation, emphasizing style and aesthetic appeal. The survey measures purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willingness to pay.. Sample: 300 work/industrial hearing protection users and 300 leisure/active consumers, randomly assigned to see either A or B.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: intent to purchase) and maximum price willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the EN 352 safety messaging (A) than for the fashion messaging (B).; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the fashion messaging (B) than for the safety messaging (A).. Decision rule: If purchase intent for the EN 352 safety messaging (A) is at least 10 percentage points higher than for the fashion messaging (B) among work/industrial users, proceed with a differentiated safety proposition. If the difference is less than 5 percentage points, do not invest. If the difference is less than 3 percentage points, consider a hybrid approach that includes both safety and fashion elements.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes EN 352 certification and safety for outdoor recreation, but first validate demand through a low-cost test. If the test shows purchase intent for the safety messaging is at least 10 percentage points higher than for the fashion messaging, proceed with a limited launch; otherwise, do not invest. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns packing errors and does not address consumer purchase intent or willingness to pay for a differentiated proposition. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safety product that meets regulatory standards, because they already use hearing protection in work and industrial settings and trust certified standards.. Why behaviour changes: Compliance and workplace safety requirements create a demand for certified protection, prompting consumers to purchase products that meet EN 352 standards.. Test "Homeowner Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 30-55 who have gardened in the past year, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) for a differentiated Deere lawn tractor at three price points ($1,500, $1,800, $2,000). 2) Primary driver ranking (convenience vs safety vs other).. Decision rule: If the WTP at the $2,000 price point exceeds $1,800 for both convenience and safety drivers, proceed with a differentiated proposition targeting both convenience and safety. Test "Homeowner vs Small-Farm Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and purchase intent questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 self-identified homeowners with small gardens and 250 small-farm owners. Recruit via panels to ensure representation.. Measure: Purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and willingness to pay a premium price (e.g., 10% above standard price).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium compared to small-farm owners.; T2: Small-farm owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium compared to homeowners.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for homeowners is at least 1.5 points higher than for small-farm owners and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a differentiated homeowner proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners with small gardens, leveraging Deere's existing dealer network and brand reputation for durability. Conduct a low‑cost purchase‑intent test to validate demand before full rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.
